about: The endpoint card's brain-map tree as data, written by gen-brainmap.js beside brainmap-endpoint.html, which embeds the same object as window.BM_DATA. Generated; never edit by hand.

head.title: A brain map for the endpoint's panels
head.lede: The inventory's 61 attributes, sorted by M1 into the 11 blocks you ruled, drawn as a tree you walk. Click a node to open its panel in the tray; click it again to close it. 9 attributes belong to 3 or more blocks at once, so they are drawn as shared and never as one branch's property.
head.keys: In the map: <kbd>Tab</kbd> reaches the tree · <kbd>←</kbd> <kbd>→</kbd> move along a level · <kbd>↑</kbd> <kbd>↓</kbd> move between levels · <kbd>Enter</kbd> or <kbd>Space</kbd> opens and closes a node · <kbd>Esc</kbd> closes the last one opened.
head.sketchNote: The sketch you drew has the root at the top right and every edge running down and to the left. Option C keeps it exactly. Option A is the same tree turned 45°, which is the turn you asked for: the diagonal becomes one straight axis.

map.title: The map
map.n: click a node to open its panel

reads.title: What it draws
reads.n: the depth is your ruling · the other counts are measured against the inventory and M1

layout.label: Placement

group.label: Grouping

spine.label: Shared attributes

keep.label: Filter
keep.plain: Keep only, as its own control: never a click on a node.

acts.label: Actions
acts.plain: Whether each node shows what a click on it would do.

A.name: Upright
A.line1: Your sketch turned 45°, so the tree hangs straight down: root at the top, the branches fanning out below it, the tray across the bottom.
A.line2: Depth reads downward and breadth reads across, so a wide level runs off to the side and the pane scrolls sideways.
A.plain: The tree hangs down from the root, and the panels sit under it.

B.name: Sideways
B.line1: The same tree turned the other way, reading left to right: the root on the left, depth growing rightward, the panels in a column on the right.
B.line2: Breadth now runs down the page, which is the direction a long list already reads — the test of whether left-to-right beats top-to-bottom for you.
B.plain: The tree grows to the right, and the panels stand beside it.

C.name: As sketched
C.line1: The diagonal exactly as you drew it: root at the top right, every edge running down and to the left at 45°.
C.line2: It is kept honestly so the turn is visible: Upright's own node positions, spread — every distance between nodes multiplied by one factor, the smallest that keeps the turned boxes clear of each other — and then turned. With nothing open that factor is {spreadClosed}; as the map stands now it is {spread}. It climbs whenever the turn alone would put boxes on top of each other: a crowded branch open, or the shared attributes drawn as a band.
C.plain: The tree runs across the corner of the page, the way you drew it.

D.name: Radial
D.line1: The root in the middle, the branches around it, depth growing outward in rings; the tray sits below the circle.
D.line2: Every branch is the same distance from the root, so none of them looks more important than another — which also means order stops carrying meaning.
D.plain: The root sits in the middle and the branches circle it.

E.name: Indented
E.line1: No drawing at all: a nested list, one line per node, indented by depth.
E.line2: The control that says whether the tree earns its space — if this reads as well, the picture is decoration.
E.plain: A plain indented list, with no picture.

flat.name: Flat
flat.plain: Every block sits directly under the root, with its attributes below it.

standpoint.name: By standpoint
standpoint.plain: The blocks gather under the standpoint each one names, in your words.

section.name: By section
section.plain: The inventory's own groups, with each attribute under the one it was written in.

stage.name: By stage
stage.plain: Your record's spine, in its order: 6 stages, then the UNCAUGHT bay that runs beside every stage, then the CLIENT screen after the answer leaves — each holding the blocks proposed for it. A proposal: nothing in the data says which rows a block touches.

nodes.name: Shared nodes
nodes.note: drawn in every block that needs it
nodes.plain: A shared attribute appears under each block that needs it, marked as shared.

band.name: One band
band.plain: Every shared attribute is lifted out into one band under the root, with a faint wire to each block that needs it.

below.name: Below
below.plain: The panels sit in a tray across the bottom, with the sweep coming down to them.

beside.name: Beside
beside.plain: The panels stand in a column at the right, with the sweep coming across to them.

on.name: Shown
on.plain: Every node carries the marks of the moves it offers, and its panel lists them.

off.name: Hidden
off.plain: The map draws names only, the way it did before the moves were proposed.

middle.name: the middle
middle.plain: The panel under the map changes to show this — the result, in the dimension you picked.

portrait.name: the portrait
portrait.plain: One thing, in full, in the panel on the right. It replaces nothing else.

map.name: the map itself
map.plain: The map redraws: what is kept stays, what is not goes quiet. Nothing new is fetched.

here.name: here
here.plain: It opens in this tray, beside what you already opened.

select.name: Show
select.plain: Puts this thing's own rows in front of you. It replaces what the region was showing, and nothing is hidden elsewhere.

filter.name: Keep only
filter.plain: Narrows what every other region shows to the things that carry this. A filter is sticky: it stays until you drop it, and the page says it is on.

open.name: Open
open.plain: Opens the one record — every field of it, with where it came from. It is a detail view, not a change of subject.

trace.name: Follow
trace.plain: Walks from this thing to what it reaches, one step at a time. It changes the subject to the step you land on.

acts.head: What a click does
acts.offersNone: No other move: a click is the only one.
acts.filterLine: Filtering is not a click. Keep only is its own control, on the rail above the map, and it says it is on until you remove it.
acts.lead: Each of these is a move, not a link: it says what changes and which part of the console answers.
acts.note: PROPOSED, not built. The map is the COMMAND region — it names concepts and never a code. Nothing here reaches the feed yet; what it would show is named so you can rule on it by looking.

ui.more: How the map knows what it draws — kept off the face on purpose.
ui.copy: Your picks as text, placed on the clipboard for pasting into the chat.

map: A branch's number is what that branch holds: attributes under Flat, By standpoint and By section — blocks under By stage, where a row holds blocks and a row holding none says so in words instead of a number. Either way a fat branch is a panel with a lot in it before you open anything.
The tray keeps what you opened in the order you opened it, so the last thing you looked at is the last panel.
9 attributes are drawn shared. Under one setting of the Shared attributes rail they sit in several branches at once; under the other they sit once, in a band. Both are the same fact drawn 2 ways.
options: Each placement draws the same 12 nodes when nothing is open. Only where they sit changes.
The widest placement needs {widest} across; the tallest needs {tallest} down. The pane scrolls rather than shrinking the type below the floor.
Indented is the control. If it answers as fast as the pictures, the pictures are spending space for nothing.

open.why: Every place the agent chose something you have not ruled. Named here rather than buried in a commit message.

items.q: Which rows of your spine each block touches, and where a block that spans rows is drawn. Nothing in the data maps a block to a row.
items.did: Proposed a list per block (D-021), over all 8 rows of your record — the 6 stages, the UNCAUGHT bay and the CLIENT screen. Blocks naming a single row: 1 · several: 6 · none: 4. D-021 as recorded puts every block whose list is not a single row under Across the stages (10 blocks), and the rows it leaves empty are: EDGE · GATE · INPUT · HANDLER · EFFECTS · ANSWER · UNCAUGHT. My pick draws each block under every row it touches, so Across holds only the blocks with an empty list (4), and the rows it leaves empty are: none. A switch under By stage shows both. 3 blocks are drawn under the bay — “Data effects” · “Endings” · “Proof” — because the 500 nobody caught is an ending they must be able to show.
items.ask: Move any block you would put elsewhere, and say which rule you keep for a block that spans rows.

items.q: You said “the four standpoints the blocks name”. The blocks name 9.
items.did: Grouped by all 9, each one read off the block's own standpoint sentence. Named by more than a single block: “what determines the path” (Endings · Gates and decisions). The blocks your standpoints do not name — 2 of them — gather in a bucket of their own, which is not a standpoint they share.
items.ask: Tell me which of them you meant, or accept 9.

items.q: Where the Keep-only control sits, and which node it keeps.
items.did: On the rail above the map, as its own group, taking the node opened last. A filter changes the map, and the rail is where the controls that change the map live; in a panel's head it would look like one of the node's moves again, and closing the panel would hide the only way to remove it.
items.ask: Say if it belongs in the panel head instead, or should keep a node you pick some other way.

items.q: Which node the sweep starts from when more than one is open.
items.did: The sweep starts at the node opened last, so it follows where you are rather than where you were.
items.ask: Say if it should stay on the first one instead.

items.did: A panel for the card as a whole: the counts, and the blocks in order of how many attributes they hold.
items.ask: Say if the root should open nothing at all.

items.q: Whether opening a second branch closes the first.
items.did: It does not. The tray grows, and a node closes only when you click it again or press Escape.
items.ask: Say if one open branch at a time reads better.

lines: The blocks are M1's: 20 questions clustered by which attributes they need, cut at the widest drop in the ladder. The cells are 1a215eb2, the inventory 11931871.
An attribute's block is the one M1 measured, never one chosen here. 52 attributes have a block of their own, 9 are shared across 3 or more, and 0 have none because they were written after the rating.

Renames declared across the second ruling: 2, of which 0 still join an attribute to M1 — the rename “rate limit” → “Rate tier” is spent, because the matrix already uses the inventory's own name; the rename “journeys workflow step” → “Workflow step” is spent, because the matrix already uses the inventory's own name. The generator stops if either side of a rename stops being true.
The standpoint groups are read off each block's own standpoint sentence in prisms-endpoint.json, by phrase, not by a list kept here.

Option C is option A's node positions turned 45°, computed, not drawn by hand — and spread before the turn, every distance between nodes multiplied by one factor, the smallest that keeps the turned boxes clear of each other. The same factor for every node is what keeps C a copy of A: turning C back by 45° gives A again exactly, at that one scale — {spread} as the map stands now, {spreadClosed} with nothing open.

pickIntro: Pick the placement you want, set the 5 switches beside it the way you want them kept, and copy the text — it records the pick and every switch by name, By stage's own extra switch included.

facts.text: The map draws 3 levels and no more, which is your ruling on the command card. A grouping that would put attributes on a fourth level does not draw them: they open in the block's panel instead, and the line under the map says how many are waiting there.
An attribute the map calls shared is needed by 3 or more of the 11 blocks. 9 attributes qualify; “The endings” is the extreme, needed by 6.
Every one of the 61 rows is claimed: 52 sit in a block of their own and 9 are shared. Nothing hangs loose, so the map draws no branch for the unplaced.
4 attributes M1 placed no longer have a row in the inventory, so they are drawn nowhere: “usage fan in” and “steps in the longest chain” and “rate limit” and “journeys workflow step”.

blocks.name: Data effects
blocks.plain: The rows the endpoint touches, the moment it touches them, and the fate of each change.
blocks.standpoint: Your first standpoint: what we read, write, modify, create and delete.
blocks.stageWhy: The data row of the topics table: users at GATE, the rest at HANDLER, the fate at ANSWER — and EFFECTS is the stage of the writes themselves. It also reaches the UNCAUGHT bay: its own question asks whether a write survived THIS ending, and on the failure nobody caught the writes are left neither committed nor rolled back.

blocks.name: Endings
blocks.plain: The ways a request can end, and the expected one among them.
blocks.standpoint: The destinations in your standpoint on what determines the path. The forks that lead to them sit in Gates and decisions.
blocks.stageWhy: Its own question asks at which stage each ending leaves, so its list is exactly the rows whose 'endings that leave here' column is not empty — 6 of them, the UNCAUGHT bay among them: the 500 nobody caught is an ending, and the bay is where it leaves.

blocks.name: Functions
blocks.plain: The code that runs, sorted by how much it decides.
blocks.standpoint: Your functions standpoint, from the one facing the API down to the little helpers.
blocks.stageWhy: The functions row of the topics table: the dependencies at GATE, the handler and its calls at HANDLER. The catches sit where they are, so they add no row of their own. The bay is NOT in its list: a raise nothing catches is a fact about the ENDING it produces, which the endings block draws there; what the functions row names is where the catches ARE.

blocks.name: In-flight state
blocks.plain: The values that stay alive only while the request runs.
blocks.standpoint: Your standpoint on what is saved temporarily and alive during the process. The map cannot read most of it yet.
blocks.stageWhy: Its own question is about what was alive DURING the process: a value set at a stage and read at a later stage lives between them, so no single row holds it.

blocks.name: Standard or specialist
blocks.plain: The pieces this endpoint is built from, set against the pieces most endpoints share.
blocks.standpoint: None of your standpoints names it. It is the common versus specialist lens from your forward ideas, and it compares endpoints instead of reading one.
blocks.stageWhy: Its own question sets the whole door against other doors; it is about the endpoint, not about any single stage of it.

blocks.name: Stages and order
blocks.plain: The stations a request passes, and the order in which things run.
blocks.standpoint: Your stage spine, read as a sequence. It is the time axis of the console.
blocks.stageWhy: Its own questions ARE the stages and their order; drawing it under any of them would make it its own child.

blocks.name: Proof
blocks.plain: The conditions a test proves, and the ones nothing reaches.
blocks.standpoint: Your coverage standpoint, the part the lab calls Tests.
blocks.stageWhy: Its own question is about conditions, and a condition ends the request at the stage its ending leaves — the tests row of the topics table says the same: the cases hang at the stage the ending leaves. The UNCAUGHT bay is in the list because its 500 is the condition nothing reaches: no case is written for it, and that absence is the answer the question wants.

blocks.name: Gates and decisions
blocks.plain: The checks that stop a request and the forks that decide its ending.
blocks.standpoint: Your standpoint on what determines the path. The part the lab calls Security lands here, because a gate is one kind of fork.
blocks.stageWhy: The security row of the topics table: the band at EDGE, the scheme and gates at GATE, the guards at HANDLER. The bay is NOT in its list: what leaves there is by definition the failure no gate decided.

blocks.name: Structures
blocks.plain: The shapes of the body that comes in and the body that goes out.
blocks.stageWhy: The schemas row of the topics table: the request shape and its 422 cases at INPUT, the response shape at ANSWER. The bay is NOT in its list: the body that leaves there is the framework's, not a shape this door declares.

blocks.name: Overview and risk
blocks.plain: The whole endpoint at a glance, and the things about it that look wrong.
blocks.standpoint: None of your standpoints names it. It is what the face and the command panel answer before any view is chosen.
blocks.stageWhy: Its own questions are about the whole door at a glance, and its risks can sit in any row, so no single row holds it.

blocks.name: Client
blocks.plain: The screen's side of each ending.
blocks.standpoint: Your reach outward standpoint, the one the lab calls widening.
blocks.stageWhy: The widening row of the topics table: the screen at CLIENT. The screen sits after the answer leaves, so it is its own row, not ANSWER's. The bay is NOT in its list: the screen must still handle the 500 that nothing translated, but it reads it after the answer leaves — at CLIENT, the row it already sits under.

stages.name: EDGE
stages.plain: The checks every request meets before it reaches this door — the app band.

stages.name: GATE
stages.plain: The lock on the door — who may knock, and what the gate provisions.

stages.name: INPUT
stages.plain: The body — can it be read, does it fit the shape.

stages.name: HANDLER
stages.plain: The door's own decisions — guards, calls, arms, catches.

stages.name: EFFECTS
stages.plain: The writes the door leaves behind — which survive each ending.

stages.name: ANSWER
stages.plain: The reply the caller gets — one body per ending, beside what was promised.

stages.name: UNCAUGHT
stages.plain: Anything nobody caught — possible at any step. It is the BAY of your record, not a step of its own: it runs beside every stage, and what leaves here is the 500 that nothing translated.

stages.name: CLIENT
stages.plain: The screen that reads the answer — can it tell the endings apart. It is the SCREEN of your record: it sits after the answer leaves, so it is a row of its own and not a part of ANSWER.

stageWords.note: The rail draws your spine: 8 rows, in your order — 6 stages, then the UNCAUGHT bay, which runs beside every stage, then the CLIENT screen, which sits after the answer leaves. Across the stages is a branch of this map, not a row of your record. What is a PROPOSAL, not a measurement, is which rows each block touches: the agent chose them from your stage record — the topics table for the topic blocks, the block's own questions for the rest. Open a block to read why; correct any of them.
stageWords.emptyPlain: No block sits under this row with the rule you picked. It is drawn anyway, dashed, because a door that has nothing at a stage still HAS the stage.

acrossPlain.one: Blocks that name several rows, or none: D-021's rule puts them here rather than forcing them onto a single row.
acrossPlain.every: Blocks that belong under no row of your spine: their lists are empty, so there is nothing to draw them under.

rule.label: A block that spans rows goes
rule.plain: Where a block that names several rows, or none, is drawn.

one.name: under Across the stages
one.note: the rule as recorded in D-021
one.plain: A block that names a single row sits under it; a block that names several, or none, sits under Across the stages.

every.name: under every stage it touches
every.plain: A block is drawn under every row in its list, so it appears more than once; only a block with an empty list sits under Across.

keep.label: Keep only
keep.plain: Takes the node you opened last and quiets every node that does not carry it. It stays on until you remove it.
keep.btnNone: Keep only — open a node first
keep.btnRoot: Keep only — the root carries everything
keep.chipOn: Keep only is ON: the map keeps what carries “{name}” ({kind}); {quiet} other nodes are quiet.
keep.chipHow: It stays on through clicks, placements and groupings. Remove it with the button beside this.
keep.offPlain: Turns Keep only off: every node comes back.

qtext.Q1: At which moment is a table touched, and on what does that depend?
qtext.Q2: On THIS ending, which tables were written, and did the write survive?
qtext.Q3: Which endings can this door produce, and at which stage does each one leave?
qtext.Q4: Which conditions of this door does a test prove, and which does nothing reach?
qtext.Q5: What should be at this stage for this topic?
qtext.Q6: Which gate stopped this request, and which ones did it pass first?
qtext.Q7: What executes after what inside the door?
qtext.Q8: What does the client do with each ending — can it tell two 409s apart?
qtext.Q9: Which tables does the door touch that the Data panel never draws?
qtext.Q10: What fields does this entity carry, and how do they hang together?
qtext.Q11: Which route is the expected one, and which are the exceptions?
qtext.Q12: Is this door built from standard pieces, or did it go specialist?
qtext.Q13: What shape goes in and what shape comes back on this ending?
qtext.Q14: Which door is the densest, the riskiest, the least tested?
qtext.Q15: Where in the code is this — can I open it?
qtext.Q16: What did the door save temporarily — cache, or something ephemeral that was alive and important during the process?
qtext.Q17: What determines the path — what makes this a 401, a 402 or a 200?
qtext.Q18: Which functions are the crucial ones: facing the API, deciding the ending, touching the database, giving context?
qtext.Q19: Which little functions sit inside the loop, and of what type (formatting · capping · validation…)?
qtext.Q20: What is inside this element, and what is there to explore — implications, effects, impact, coverage?

Q1+Q2+Q9.why: The data row of the topics table: users at GATE, the rest at HANDLER, the fate at ANSWER — and EFFECTS is the stage of the writes themselves. It also reaches the UNCAUGHT bay: its own question asks whether a write survived THIS ending, and on the failure nobody caught the writes are left neither committed nor rolled back.
Q1+Q2+Q9.cites: | data | the tables touched at each stage — the WHEN picture (users at GATE, the rest at HANDLER, the fate at ANSWER)

Q3+Q11.why: Its own question asks at which stage each ending leaves, so its list is exactly the rows whose 'endings that leave here' column is not empty — 6 of them, the UNCAUGHT bay among them: the 500 nobody caught is an ending, and the bay is where it leaves.
Q3+Q11.cites: | Q3 | Which endings can this door produce, and at which stage does each one leave?

Q15+Q18+Q19.why: The functions row of the topics table: the dependencies at GATE, the handler and its calls at HANDLER. The catches sit where they are, so they add no row of their own. The bay is NOT in its list: a raise nothing catches is a fact about the ENDING it produces, which the endings block draws there; what the functions row names is where the catches ARE.
Q15+Q18+Q19.cites: | functions | the dependencies at GATE, the handler and its calls at HANDLER, the catches where they are

Q16.why: Its own question is about what was alive DURING the process: a value set at a stage and read at a later stage lives between them, so no single row holds it.
Q16.cites: | Q16 | What did the door save temporarily

Q12.why: Its own question sets the whole door against other doors; it is about the endpoint, not about any single stage of it.
Q12.cites: | Q12 | Is this door built from standard pieces, or did it go specialist?

Q5+Q7.why: Its own questions ARE the stages and their order; drawing it under any of them would make it its own child.
Q5+Q7.cites: | Q5 | What should be at this stage for this topic?

Q4.why: Its own question is about conditions, and a condition ends the request at the stage its ending leaves — the tests row of the topics table says the same: the cases hang at the stage the ending leaves. The UNCAUGHT bay is in the list because its 500 is the condition nothing reaches: no case is written for it, and that absence is the answer the question wants.
Q4.cites: | Q4 | Which conditions of this door does a test prove, and which does nothing reach?

Q6+Q17.why: The security row of the topics table: the band at EDGE, the scheme and gates at GATE, the guards at HANDLER. The bay is NOT in its list: what leaves there is by definition the failure no gate decided.
Q6+Q17.cites: | security | the band at EDGE, the scheme and gates at GATE, the guards at HANDLER — passed or fired

Q10+Q13.why: The schemas row of the topics table: the request shape and its 422 cases at INPUT, the response shape at ANSWER. The bay is NOT in its list: the body that leaves there is the framework's, not a shape this door declares.
Q10+Q13.cites: | schemas | the request shape at INPUT, the response shape at ANSWER, the 422 cases at INPUT

Q14+Q20.why: Its own questions are about the whole door at a glance, and its risks can sit in any row, so no single row holds it.
Q14+Q20.cites: | Q14 | Which door is the densest, the riskiest, the least tested?

Q8.why: The widening row of the topics table: the screen at CLIENT. The screen sits after the answer leaves, so it is its own row, not ANSWER's. The bay is NOT in its list: the screen must still handle the 500 that nothing translated, but it reads it after the answer leaves — at CLIENT, the row it already sits under.
Q8.cites: | widening | the screen at CLIENT — the reason site, the guard chain, the hook's moves
